text: — Don't give me all that chatter, I'm telling you we must elect the government's men! — shouted Bay Ganyo and struck the table hard.
— But how are we going to elect pro-government ones, where will we dig up voters from? Why, you, Bai Ganyo, aren't you... supposedly a liberal — Bochoolu dared to object.
— Who told you that I am a liberal! — Bay Ganyo asked sternly.

— What do you mean who told me? Why, don't you remember how many conservatives you've thrashed, how much you've cursed them, so how could you not be a liberal? Don't you know — you said it yourself — that you even bragged to Jireček that you were a liberal? — Bochoolu objected.

— Oh, how simple you are! — Bay Ganyo replies with a condescending smile. — So what if I told Jireček that, does a word make a hole! Listen, you fool, if I don't trick a Jireček, who else am I going to trick?
— You are right, your honor! Bochoolu, keep your head down, don't nag him! — Gochoolu spoke up. — I am a conservative too.

— Why, am I a stone on a grave! I, for one, am a total conservative — blurted out Dochoolu, — come on, you become a conservative too, Bochoolu, so we can grab those fellows so they won't be able to budge.
— "Alright, but I don't know who the manager will be with," Bochoolu replies.

— The governor? With our people, of course — reports Bay Ganyo, — and the district governor is with us too. The standing commission isn't legal, but who's going to look for legality? It's ours. The bureau is ours. The city council is ours. The mayor is fidgeting a bit, but we'll cut his tail short. The municipal councils in the villages haven't been confirmed on purpose, do you understand? If they're with us — we'll confirm them, if not — to hell with them. I tell you again — as for the governor, don't you worry, he's ours.
— What about the porters? — Bochoolu inquired curiously.
— The porters are ours, and the gypsies, and Danko the Scoundrel is ours...
— But wasn't he in prison for theft? — Bochoolu wondered.

— Heh, you’re grazing ducks. We let him loose, we did. After all, he’s the one who won the porters over for us. He went to them the other day, gathered them, and when he gnashed his teeth at them, they froze in their tracks; when he growled at them: “I’ll smash your teeth in if you don’t elect Bay Ganyo!” — and the porters gave in. Danko bargained with them for two leva a head and, on the eve of the elections, food and drink all night long.
— A fearsome rebel, wow!

— And for how much, do you think! For 50 leva. He went to those people to ask for 100 leva, they kicked him out, they berated him. You'll see him this Sunday — he'll crush their bones! — says Bay Ganyo smugly.
— Bochoolu, go and call Gunya the Lawyer to come here and write us an appeal, tell him: “Bai Ganyo is calling you.”

As soon as Bochoolu went out, Bay Ganyo lowered his head and in a mysterious voice turned to his companions:
— Keep quiet! We’ll keep lying to this fool until the very day of the elections that we’ll make him a deputy; we’ll write a few ballots with his name just for show, and the other ballots will be written by the clerks in the City Council and the District Administration. Now listen to me: the minister wants me to be a deputy without fail. You, Gochoolu, do you want to?
— Well, I'd like to, Bai Ganyo — replies Gochoolu.
— I'd like to as well — says Dochoolu.

"Well, you’d like that, wouldn’t you, but to tell you the truth, you’ve completely disgraced yourself before the people. Why did you have to put yourself so much on display; who was shouting in the squares: 'Long live the great patriot!', 'Down with the foul tyrant!', 'To the gallows with Kliment!', 'Long live Kliment!'?"
— But weren't we always together, Bai Ganyo, why are you being dishonest?

— Together, but our dealings are always hush-hush. Finally, oh well, since you want it so much—fine, I’ll choose you. The fact that the peasants hate you and you’ve sold their very rugs with your wretched usury...
— As for that, don't you talk, Bay Ganyo, don't I know what sort you are too — Dochoolu said cautiously.

Bay Ganyo is ready to boil over, but at that moment Gunyo the Lawyer enters. Bay Ganyo explains to him what the proclamation should be like. Gunyo sits at the table, takes the pen, and immerses himself in thought. At Bay Ganyo's order, the servant brings a bottle of mastic. Gochoolu, Dochoolu, and Bay Ganyo drink, Gunyo writes. After half an hour, the following is ready:
APPEAL TO THE VOTERS OF OUR DISTRICT

In view of the great importance and significance that the upcoming elections for people's representatives hold for the present and future of our fatherland, we, the citizens, numbering more than 700 people, gathered today in the courtyard of the school in Partsal Mahlesi, and having discussed the matter of the candidacies of the persons for representatives, we reached an agreement and unanimously decided to recommend to the Messrs. voters of our district as people's representatives our fellow citizens:
Ganyo Balkanski, a merchant famous throughout Bulgaria.
Filyu Gochoolu, a merchant with capital.
Tanas Dochoolu, merchant in the wine industry.
Precisely the same persons whom the committee of the People's Party had recommended to you with its appeal of August 27 of last month.

As we announce this unanimous decision of ours to the rest of the Messrs. voters of our city and district, who have at heart the good of the Fatherland, the material improvement of the farmer, the relief of the taxpayer's situation, in a word, the interests of our district, we urge them to cast their votes in the election on the 11th of this month for the above three fellow citizens of ours, in whom we have full confidence that they will represent our country with dignity in the National Assembly.
Dear Voters,

A list has already been presented to you by several citizens with the names of Nikola Tarnovaliyata, Lulcho Doktorov, and Ivanitsa Gramatikov—individuals not from our circle, individuals foreign to us, who do not and cannot have our trust. Perhaps others will also appear to persuade you to vote for their candidates. We advise you, Messrs. voters, not to be deceived by their fine words, and do not yield to their flatteries, and do not believe the various rumors and fabrications spread by them regarding some sort of district telegrams and so forth. Nikola Tarnovaliyata is a native of the city of Tarnovo, and therefore, out of spite, he burns the quilt for the sake of a flea. Lulcho Doktorov is through and through "Trans-Danubian Governorate," while nobody knows Ivanitsa Gramatikov and, nota bene, he is a Russian graduate, and therefore a traitor to our dear Fatherland.
Dear Voters,
We are convinced that the above persons, i.e. the following:
Ganyu Balkanski,
Filyu Gochoolu,
Tanas Dochoolu,

those who have full devotion and prostrate loyalty to THE THRONE AND THE DYNASTY OF HIS ROYAL HIGHNESS OUR BELOVED PRINCE FERDINAND I and who will faithfully support our current patriotic government headed by the current Prime Minister, will win your trust.
— Bravo, Gunyo — exclaimed Bay Ganyo, — you're a regular Bismarck.
— What, do you take me for a fool? — Gunyo spoke up smugly.
— Now go and take this to the printing house to have it printed in large letters, like these!
— And this money?

— There's no money, you tell him to print it like that; if not, tell him we'll tell the City Council and the other offices not to have their papers printed by him. Got it? Off you go now — Bay Ganyo commanded.
— Do you know — continued Bay Ganyo, — those people sent a telegram to the minister to complain to him that the governor has gone around the villages to campaign.
— Fools! — calls out Gochoolu.
— And what ones! — Dochoolu added.
— The Minister is not the Holy Virgin, to listen to them just like that! He answered them: the elections are free, ha-ha-ha!...
— Ha-ha-ha! — Gochoolu and Dochoolu giggle.

— A terrible devil, damn him. Freedom? There’s your freedom! They’ll see such freedom on Sunday that they’ll remember it for the rest of their lives. Especially Gramatikov! He, poor soul, hasn't seen our elections yet. Just let those Vlachs of mine come out against him, those Gypsies of mine with bloodshot eyes, bulging out two fingers' width, those hoarse throats, those sashes up to their necks; let them glare at him, and then let that wild boar, Danko the Scoundrel, come up behind him and just shout: "Grab him!"
— Ha-ha-ha! — Gochoolu and Dochoolu giggle, their eyes lit up with pleasure.

— Li-be-rals! Con-sti-too-shun! There, con-sti-too-shun! They are always hoping for the "circular telegram." They’ve deafened people’s ears with this circular telegram. They keep reading it, they keep pointing it out to the world. How we laughed yesterday with the governor in the café. He, just for show, had that damn telegram printed and sent it out to the cafés. Yesterday we were sitting with him in the café, watching those guys, their heads bowed over a table like sheep resting at noon, reading and reading the telegram, rejoicing, we hear them whispering: "Free! The elections are free! The police won't interfere!" And us with the governor, tee-hee-hee! I look at him with one eye and say to him jokingly: "We are sure!" He starts giggling and—hop—a mastika. He pats his pocket—meaning that letter about the freedom of the elections—winks and says: "We are not sure," and tee-hee-hee! Hop! Another mastika... We got good and plastered!... Then Danko the Thief came, and others, and others, and we locked ourselves in the café, and I shouted to the violinists: now then! They snapped their strings!... Georgi's mastika isn't good, and the appetizer is lousy; he doesn't bother to make pickles, but gives sour okra instead!... Ugh! My head hurts from yesterday. Gochoolu, pour another round of mastika.
— To the hangover!
— Don't even mention it, we have to drink again tonight. Starting tonight, we have to station the men in the taverns.
"Isn't it early, Bay Ganyo?" spoke up Dochooolu.

— It’s not early, tomorrow is Saturday, they have 36 hours left to drink. It’s not early! Perfect! And finally, they won’t all be drinking at once. They will take turns. Some will drink for 5–6 hours, they’ll rest, others will start. In order, in order! Once they gather, they won’t disperse. They’ll drink there, they’ll eat there, they’ll sleep there! Do you understand?
— We know, is it the first time we're holding elections! — Gochooolu says.

— You, Gochoolu, when you pass by the Arnaut, tell him to prepare 300 okas of bread for tonight and send them — 100 okas to the Gypsy quarter to Topachoolu, 100 okas to Partsal Mahala at Gogo’s tavern, and 100 okas down to the porters. You, Dochoolu, go by those taverns and tell them to start giving out wine and rakia starting tonight. Let them give them more rakia, do you hear? And tell them not to overcharge too much, or the devils will take them. The year before last, those scoundrels plucked 2000 leva from us for next to nothing! Tell them to watch themselves, because the City Council is ours! Go by the butchers too, tell them to gather whatever offal, liver, intestines, and bones they have into one or two baskets, so we can send them to the taverns to boil a cauldron of soup for our people. Tonight the governor and the district chief will return from the villages; I’ll take them with me to make the rounds of the other taverns and cafes. We’ll gather people from all the offices to write ballots; we’ll make them write all night. I chose the paper, sort of grayish, yellowish. We’ll fold our ballots like amulets...
— Three-cornered ones — explains Dochoolu.

— The Three-cornered ones. We need to get hold of a few of their ballots, to see what their paper is like and how they fold them, so I can have the scribes write 1,000–2,000 ballots on their paper with our names.
"— You’re a hell of a devil, Bai Ganyo, you know these damn things like the back of your hand! — says Gochoolu with reverence."

— A fine business! Why am I Ganyo Balkanski if I don't know this trade too? You, my dear sir, put me in whichever district you want and tell me whoever you want me to elect for you. Put up a donkey as a candidate, and I'll elect the donkey for you, damn it all! Just give me the district chief with the gendarmes and give me 1,000–2,000 leva. Let me gather for you, my friend, those rascals of yours, the scum of the earth, some 40–50 jailbirds, and line them up in two or three taverns on the outskirts, put a bucket of wine before each head, and then shout to them: "Come on then! Long live Bulgaria!" Heh! Are you there, Penka!... When those bulging eyes of theirs get bloodshot, when they start pulling those knives of theirs from their belts, stabbing them into the tables, when they raise a hullabaloo with those hoarse, raspy voices—it'll make your skin crawl! Then take and lead this horror through the middle of town at night... Opposition?... The devil himself wouldn't dare face you! Lead them past the house of some opponent... Good heavens! When they open those throats of theirs!... You'll hear them from an hour's distance away, ants will crawl under your skin, your hair will stand on end like a hedgehog's!... Then summon the village mayors and clerks, then flash your eyes at them, then gnash your teeth at them, then point out those rascals to them... Voters?... — You won't even see their shadows! When 12 municipal councilors from every village land there along with the mayors, when you gather the officials and clerks, place gendarmes at the edges to turn back the other peasants, surround the polling station with those 40–50 cutthroats, pull some trickery, stuff several bundles of ballots into the boxes, and there's your donkey as a Member of Parliament, ha-ha-ha!
— Ha-ha-ha — responded Gochoolu and Dochoolu, — bravo, Bay Ganyo!
— That's right, but the police alone aren't enough; the bureau must be yours as well — Gochoolu added.
— I think so too — Dochoolu added. — It is ours now, but I’m saying, as it were... Really, Bay Ganyo, do tell us, please, how did you manage to pull off this bureau?

— How so? — Bay Ganyo responds with a self-satisfied smile. — Quite simple! Didn't we elect a district council? Eight turned out to be theirs, four — ours. We had four of theirs annulled, the more prominent ones... But you'll say that a hullabaloo was raised. To hell with it! By the time they sort it out — the elections will be over. We were left with four of theirs and four of ours. But from theirs, we only left the nobodies. We gathered to elect a standing committee. The messenger couldn't find one of theirs — do you get it?
— Tsk... tsk... tsk...! — clicked Dochoolu. — What Bismarck! Bismarck couldn't even turn your slippers!

— Wait a minute, what have you even seen yet? And after all, are the Germans the only ones who have a Bismarck?... Anyway: we were left, efendim, three of theirs, four of ours—a majority! Well, of course, we aren't wet behind the ears—the commission turned out entirely ours. Never mind that, but our side got even more votes, because we had promised two of theirs individually that we would elect them as member-secretaries, and they, the fools, kept voting and voting for our people... ha-ha-ha! Now they walk the streets like opium-eaters. Especially one of them, an influential scoundrel—we took him to the villages to campaign with us, promising we'd elect him secretary, and he, the blockhead, went and quit his job... Abandoning the tame to chase the wild. Fool!... Dochoolu, pour another round of mastic.
Bay Ganyo strained the mastic through his mustache, wiped himself with his palm, twirled "those damn things" and continued:

— Now let me tell you how an election board is chosen. This is done by lot. The chairman of the court draws it. That’s what they call "by lot," but I can choose whoever I want for you. And it’s quite easy: if you put the slips in a glass so they can be seen from the outside, you have to make a small ink mark on the "full" slips; if, on the other hand, they are in a box, you must take a deeper box so the slips cannot be seen from the side, and you will arrange the full ones on one side and the empty ones on the other. After that, all you have to do is whisper to the chairman that "he’s in a fix" and therefore "to keep his eyes open"... They call out: Ivan, Stoyan, Parvan! Do you need Parvan? — take a full slip. Don’t you need Parvan? — take an empty slip. In other words, the chairman draws the lot...
— That damn Bay Ganyo! And those fools found someone to fight with. Woe to them — uttered Gochoolu.
"And with a head like that, you haven't become a minister yet!" — Dochooolu wonders.
— Anyway, drop it! — says Bay Ganyo modestly. — You know what Bulgarians are like!...

In the east, the dawn is barely breaking, scattering a pale light into the interior of Gogo’s tavern in Partsal Mahalesi. About thirty choice heroes are sprawled across the tables, on the floor, and over chairs; a snoring, as if thirty tigers were locked in a struggle, can be heard from the street, troubling the ears of the police sentry. From time to time, one of these heroes rises with half-closed eyes, steps over the corpses, fumbles for the pitcher, and thirstily extinguishes the alcoholic fire parching his stomach, throat, mouth, and cracked lips; those he steps upon in the darkness awaken and pour out curses and oaths from hoarse, parched throats. Stench! A hellish stench issues from their breath, poisoning the already tainted air of the tavern, saturated with the vapors of this mass of somber heroes.

Gochoolu and Dochoolu are already awake and drinking coffee in Kelesh Hasan’s café. It is time now to wake the sleeping camps of the electoral army. Here they are already in front of Gogo’s tavern. They open the doors, and a wave of suffocating stench pushes them back.
— Phew! May the devil take them! — cries Gochoolu in a choked voice and holds his nose.
— Who knows if they've been eating garlic! — Dochoolu hisses with a sour grimace and also plugs his nose.
Through the open doors, fresh air rushes into the pub and allows the not-so-sensitive pair to penetrate inside.
— Are you still sleeping, you cattle? Get up quickly! — Gochoolu commands authoritatively and starts kicking the drunken crew with his feet.
— Gogo, give them a rakia each to open their eyes — Dochoolu added.

Gogo gets up lazily from his bed, stretches, yawns, scratches himself on the sweaty spots and starts reluctantly rummaging between the bottles and glasses. The rakia, poured, he offers to the unawakened heroes.
— Get up, you donkey, here, stuff your face! Stop yawning like a dog. Just look at your eyes — bulging like boils! Come on, swallow!

With such pleasantries, aided also by energetic kicks, Gogo goes around the guests, stiff from drunkenness, and offers them rakia to bring them to their senses. Here and there, someone would growl in protest against Gogo's kicks, another would glare at him with fierce, bloodshot eyes, and someone would even make an attempt to leap up and grab the handle of the fisherman's knife tucked into his belt. These fearsome movements instill rapture in the souls of Gochoolu and Dochoolu. They whisper to each other:
— Dochoolu, look at that big fellow over there in the corner with the bandaged eye, do you know him?

— How could I not know him — Petrescu, who drowned his father in the swamp! I know him! God forbid you cross him! Do you see what a knife he has tucked in! And do you know that one there, under the counter?
— That fat one, the one bandaging the wound on his leg?
— No, the other one, with the torn mouth.
— I can't think of it... Ha, wait, wasn't it Sersem Petsa's bastard, the one who robbed the church?

— No, it isn't. Sersem Petsino is that one over there, lying next to Hayduk Boncho, and this one is Danko the Thief's grandson. Bay Ganyo sent him here to watch these vagabonds, lest   t h e   o t h e r s   deceive them. A formidable rogue! Wasn't it he who stole a bundle of   t h e i r   ballots the other night.
— Bravo!

— Do you know what we've designated him for? When we storm around the bureau, if any of theirs show up, this kid will grab Nikola Tarnovaliyata by the collar and start shouting: "Hold him! This one is insulting the Prince! He's cursing the Prince, hold him!" Then Petresku and Danko the Scoundrel will grab Nikola and throw him outside. The police will take him and — into the slammer. Theirs will want to rescue him, we — will be against them. There will be a clash. The police will rush in and scatter them like chicks. It is all arranged.
— And who will touch Lulcha and Gramatikova?
— Do you really consider them people? If someone like Topachooglu were to glare at them—they’d vanish into thin air.

Such is the conversation Gochoolu and Dochoolu are having as they observe with rapture the lazy awakening of these thirty shady characters, riff-raff gathered from the gallows, who today face the task of intimidating, driving away, and instilling terror and trembling around the polling place, and forcing the already intimidated Bulgarian to renounce his scarcely realized right to exercise his free will in the governance of the state. Such is the conversation Gochoolu and Dochoolu are having as they look at these thirty fearsome figures—disfigured, bloated, with bulging bloodshot eyes, wounded, scratched, with wide sashes and knives in their belts, with ferocity on their faces and criminal convulsions in their movements—they look at them and anticipate the sweetness of the electoral victory.

All the hired hands were already on their feet when music was heard coming from the Gypsy quarter... Music! Should I describe this music that had been performing all night in Topachooglu’s tavern, to which the tavern-keeper himself had writhed and sung: “Vangelito, embroidered kerchief, sinned upon the kerchief; oh thunder, God, strike me down and take me sooner.” Should I describe the violinist, asleep on his feet, with his violin lazily propped almost against his belly? Should I tell you about the clarinetist, who either doesn't play at all, or else blows into his clarinet like a madman, puffing out his face until the veins on his neck bulge, his bloodshot eyes pop, and it seems to you that with just a little more strain, a terrible epileptic fit will stun the listeners? No, I will not describe the music to you, for I think it sufficient to tell you only that these musicians were *à la* Bay Ganyo.

The music was playing the Pecheneg March... Amidst the intermittent sounds, a wild, a mixed roar split the air. A whole cloud of birds timidly left the trees and the eaves of Partsal Mahala. If an army of hungry lions were to face an army of provoked tigers and, at a single signal, these armies were to rush at each other, the roar that would shatter the battlefield would be similar to the wild roar that now frightened the inhabitants of the Gypsy quarter and Partsal Mahala. This was a "hurrah" from the mercenaries gathered by Danko Harsizina. There they are, appearing from the bend in the street and pouring out onto the square.

The music in front, behind the music the Gypsies and the porters. At the head, lifted on hands, with curled mustaches, with a tilted hat... who do you think? — None other than your Uncle Ganyo Balkanski. Even at this solemn moment, Uncle Ganyo does not forget himself: he keeps his hands in his pockets: “Of course, some rogue might reach in — there goes the purse. I know my own kind.” A second “hurrah,” capable of waking even the dead, deafened the ears of Gogo’s gang, which poured out of the tavern onto the square and responded with a cannonade: “Long live Uncle Ganyo!”
— Good morning, boys — shouted the beaming Bay Ganyo condescendingly.
A jumble of thirty hoarse "good mornings" responded to his greeting.

"Courage, boys, strength is with us," Bay Ganyo encourages them with the tone of Napoleon before Austerlitz. "Listen here, Danko's grandson, do you remember what I told you: when you find yourself in a tight spot, grab the man from Tarnovo by the collar and shout: 'He's cursing the Prince.' Do you understand?"
— I know — Danko’s grandson calls out cheerfully from the ranks. — And as for you, Danko, and you, Petrescu...
— We know... upside down — said Petrescu with full awareness of the importance of his task.

— Bravo! Now listen here, Petrescu, I want one more trick from you: when you get into a fight with the voters, you just stab two or three with the knife, just enough to stun them, then go ahead and throw the knife aside, then go ahead and tear your shirt at the chest, then after that, go ahead and make your skin bleed, do you understand? Then go ahead and smear your face with blood, do you understand? Then after that, start shouting that the citizens wanted to slaughter you because you were shouting: "Long live the Prince," do you understand?
— I understood, but you'll give me five more leva for blood money.
— As for money—it's easy, you just do what I tell you," Bay Ganyo reassures him.

The scouts Adamcho Kokosharina, Spiro Kopoya, and Topal Mustafa, sent on reconnaissance from the Gypsy quarter toward the polling station, arrived quickly at the square and reported to Bay Ganyo that about three thousand peasants had arrived in the town via various roads and the Tarnovaliya’s people had distributed ballots to them. “The district chief said to hurry, for the game is up.”

"To hell with your district chief!" shouted Bay Ganyo. "Why the devil did we appoint him chief if he can't even intimidate a few peasants? Chief! Rubbish! He only knows how to harass the peasant women. Fool! Why hasn't he sent gendarmes to the outskirts? The donkey has stuffed his face so much that he's forgotten what he's supposed to do. Run quickly and tell him to gather the mounted gendarmes and have them gallop through the middle of town, do you understand? Through the middle of town, flying like a whirlwind, do you hear? And then we'll give a 'hurrah' from here, and we'll see which peasant will dare stand against us. Run quickly!"

— Gogo, bring some rakia over here — Bay Ganyo commands. — Gorge yourselves, damn it, I'm paying. Why are the violinists silent? Play, you Gypsies! Blow that clarinet, why are you staring at me like an ox? That's it! Yee-hee-ha-ha!
— Danko, hand out a bundle of ballots to everyone now! Come on now, boys, forward. Courage! Long live His Royal Highness, hurrah!...
— Hooraaaa!...
And off they went... the voters!

Ivanitsa Gramatikov, the opposition candidate, woke up at six o'clock in the morning. He dressed, drank his coffee, and went out onto the high veranda in front of the house. The sun, having just risen, was reflected in the dome of the church and in the windows facing east. All of nature seemed triumphant. In fact, nature remained just as indifferent as it always is, and only the candidate's soul was triumphant.

Young, educated, a bit of an idealist, more of a dreamer, with love in his heart, with faith in the good, with hope for the future, he was not yet hardened in reality, in life. Carefree to the point of self-oblivion, an incorrigible optimist, accustomed to looking at everything from its good side, he was trusting to the point of naivety, to the point of folly.

A few friends proposed his candidacy for Member of Parliament; a meeting of citizens accepted this candidacy sympathetically, and Gramatikov thought that everything was already settled and began to drift into dreams of his forthcoming activity in the National Assembly. Milk and honey flowed across Bulgaria. But certain other details, certain preparatory actions by his friends preceding the election—actions not provided for in the electoral law—seemed to cast a shadow every now and then over his sweet dreams. Why did he have to present his program to the voters now, as if it were not possible to do without it? Why did he have to endure so many awkward moments, to answer, to promise assistance in satisfying needs that perhaps interested only the questioners? It was as if he had entrusted his entire intellect to the surrounding staff of friends! They told him he had to give a speech, and he gave a speech. They told him he had to receive the village mayors and speak to them kindly, and he received the mayors and the clerks in his house and spoke to them so kindly that the peasants lowered their eyes and hardly understood him. They expressed their needs, he took notes and sincerely stated what could be satisfied and what could not, to the extreme displeasure of the peasants, who were accustomed to being promised mountains of gold. He had to participate in the meetings of prominent citizens, in which meetings the agitators for the villages and city neighborhoods were determined and assigned. The citizens argued and made noise; he sat aside and remained silent, as if it did not concern him. This stupid passivity troubled him; he opened his mouth to say something, to object, but someone from the staff would catch him by the hand and say to him in a fatherly, patronizing tone: "You keep quiet, stay aside, you don't understand these things yet." And he would fall silent submissively and listen to the solid and self-assured conversations of the respectable citizens. "Is it always like this with elections," he thought, "or is this perhaps just beginning, with the new era?" He nudged one of the disputants and whispered in his ear: "Please, is it always like this with elections?" The disputant, preoccupied with another conversation, looked at him as if through a fog and said to him with a smile, patronizingly: "Leave that for another time; you don't understand these things, stay aside: everything is in order."

Everything is in order! Gramatikov grew accustomed to the thought that everything was in order. Wherever he sat, wherever he stood, whomever he met—be it merchant, craftsman, or peasant—he always heard the same thing: that everything was in order. If he went to the café, friends would surround him, rushing to give him news from the town and the villages: “Oh, good morning, Mr. Ivanitsa, how are you? Now everything is finally in order.” “Oh, Mr. Ivanitsa, it’s done! I could pull the whole district out of my pocket for you. Enjoy yourself! Everything is now completely in order!” If he went for an evening stroll in the city garden, friends would meet him in every alley and signal to him from afar—meaning it was done, everything is in order...

Work is in order! But an incident, of which he was an eyewitness on the eve of the elections, made him understand that there is a difference between the elections outlined in the electoral law and the elections in reality. A friend of his reminded him of this incident with the following words in a letter: “Legality, order, freedom, our success... Do you remember, do you remember? — A hullabaloo! Do you remember the invasion of the Huns into the café on the evening before the elections? Do you remember that ‘Bulgarian citizen’ with the Russian cap on the back of his head, with bare chest, barefoot, with torn knees? And that one with the red eyes, in his shirt, bareheaded, with the big cudgel in his hand? And the Vlach outside in front of the door, who in the valiant ‘intoxication’ of patriotism, in the deep consciousness of his free civil rights and duties, mature, that is, already ripened in political wisdom, could barely stand on his feet? Do you remember how from a chest, swollen with the most noble and philanthropic ideas, worthy of making a whole world happy, with a tongue thickened by the strain of the inexpressible and sublime thoughts that agitated his brain, do you remember him declaiming about freedom and people's rights, so that when an older citizen coming out of the café shouted at him, the freedom and people's rights got stuck in his throat, just as they got stuck somewhere in the noble soul of his moral fellow-partisan and chief? And this rabble, this dregs from the mire of a wild, bestial civil layer, devoid of any education or upbringing, ready for any brutality, which I could not even imagine existed in our city, self-satisfied with its ‘civilization’ and ‘Europeanness,’ this unprincipled mob, led by various ignoramuses and spineless characters who have neither principles nor can have them; and this rabble, I say, has its representatives in the National Assembly, while the thousands of voters...”

And so, on Sunday, on election day, around seven o'clock in the morning, Gramatikov stood on the high veranda of the house and, with lightness and joy, took in the morning coolness. The electoral law, brought to life in his dreams, depicted for him in succession the various moments of a constitutional election. The town clock, as it announced the half-hour with two strikes of the bell, interrupted the candidate's sweet dreams and reminded him that it was time to head to the polling station. He dressed, took his cane, but remembered that it was forbidden to enter the polling place with any kind of weapon, left his cane behind, and set off... The streets were almost empty; the people had already flocked toward the school yard. In the square in front of the church, a group of friends met him with friendly greetings:
— Oh, Mr. Ivanitsa, good morning. Did we see them?
— Whom?
— The voters. Three thousand peasants alone. We have already handed out ballots to them. Everything is in order. Now, let's go to the school.

They turned through a narrow, winding street and emerged near the polling station. Indeed, a whole mass of citizens and peasants were buzzing peacefully and quietly in the courtyard and the adjacent street. The agitators were scurrying among them and, semi-openly and semi-secretly, were handing out ballots to the newcomers. Here and there, exclamations were heard that for years on end they had not appeared at an election.
— Well, damn it, for the first time in eight years, today I am running for election.
— Me too.
— Me too.
Such confessions were heard from everywhere.

The bureau was already established in the school hall. Some voters, as well as one of the opposition candidates, were loitering around the bureau. The election began. To Gramatikov, it seemed a strange circumstance that in the yard adjacent to the school, as well as in the yards on the opposite side of the street, numerous heavily armed gendarmes were swarming, among whom two bailiffs were scurrying and whispering some instructions to them. "But isn't it forbidden by the electoral law to have an armed force in the vicinity of the polling station! Strange!"

But there was not much room left for wonder... Before Gramatikov's eyes, there began, swirled, rustled, and roared such a whirlwind of horrors and violence that he was petrified, as if struck by lightning. Here is what happened: not yet having managed to recover from the strange impression made on him by the presence of armed force around the polling station—he saw Adamcho Kokoshkarina run up to one of the police bailiffs and, breathless and frantic, whisper something confusedly into his ear. The bailiff called a gendarme, said a few words to him, and sent him off. A minute later, the district chief appeared. Adamcho whispered something to him. The district chief gave some orders to the bailiffs; they ran off, and before long—gendarmes began to emerge from the neighboring houses, leading horses behind them. They mounted the horses, the district chief at the head with a drawn saber, commanded "forward!" and twenty mounted gendarmes, armed to the teeth, rushed through the narrow street, clogged with voters, rushed in and began to tear through the living wall with the chests of their horses. Shouts, screams, uproar, protests, commands, sabers; glinting in the sun, waves of people surged back and forth, the horses cut disorderly into the crowd, the living wall split to make way for them; new waves from the back rows surged forward and pushed back the gendarmes with their mass... But the weapons prevailed, the living wall wavered. The Turkish voters began to slip away one by one: "I don't need to get beaten." The peasants began to look at one another. The gendarmes succeeded in pushing back the majority of the voters to a significant distance.

The other, very small part remained in the schoolyard. Here were Tarnovaliyata and Gramatikov. From the opposite side of the street, the shriek of a clarinet began to cut the air, violins were heard, the noise of an approaching crowd was heard, and a wild thunder shook the surroundings. Here they are: the violinists, behind them with lightning in his eyes Bay Ganyo Balkanski, here are Gochoolu and Dochoolu, here is Petrescu, the grandson of Danko Harsizina, Spiro Kopoya, Topal Mustafa, here are the gypsies, the fishermen, here is Danko Harsizina himself... — Long live the honorable government, hurrah! — shouted Danko's grandson in a thin voice.
— Hurrah... rah... raaaa! — roared the hundred-mouthed terrifying crowd.
Shivers ran through Gramatikov. The year 1876 flashed through his mind, the bashi-bazouk hordes were resurrected before him; the name of Fazli Pasha stopped on his lips.

The wild horde of drunken monsters burst into the schoolyard. My God! What coarseness, what arrogance, what dull ferocity in those bulging bloodshot eyes, in those thuggish movements, in those provocative looks!... Bay Ganyo, accompanied by his retinue, which roughly cleared a path for him, ascended the stairs and slipped into the school hall, near the desk. A noise was heard through the windows, a muffled growl, and pushed by the surging wave, Nikola Tarnovaliyata appeared on the stairs. Immediately, Danko’s grandson rushed toward him like a bird of prey and, grabbing him by the collar, began to scream at the top of his hoarse voice: “Hold him, he’s cursing the Prince, he’s insulting the Prince, hold him!” Petrescu and Danko the Thief were not far behind. Like two wolves, they seized him, hoisted him up, and dragged him down the stairs. Bay Ganyo slipped into the hall, took a note from the chairman at the desk, and handed it to Danko’s grandson, who squeezed through the crowd and slipped into the neighboring yard; a minute later, when foot and mounted gendarmes stormed into the yard, they found Bay Ganyo’s army cornered in a nook by the indignant voters who had remained in the yard. Petrescu, with a bloodied chest and blood-stained hands and face, was wailing like the most innocent babe. He had already stabbed two or three voters and managed just in time to carry out the plan—to get himself bloodied, climb onto a pile of stones, and shout for help as loud as his voice would allow: “They killed me, Mr. Chief, they were going to kill me! I’m shouting ‘Long live the Prince,’ and they’re stabbing me with knives!”

The police began their role... "Sabers out!"... The sabers clattered, the whips lashed. Protests were heard, drowned out by curses. The police, aided by Bay Ganyo’s army, hauled away Nikola Tarnovaliyata, hauled away his more prominent comrades; the mounted gendarmes charged and swept the courtyard.

And Gramatikov, swept along by the current of the crowd, found himself on the street. He was as if struck by lightning! In his ears rang the words of Bay Ganyo, who was shouting from the top of the stairs: "We too have been in Europe more or less, and we know those wretched things, the elections. I have been to Belgium..."

Grandfather Dobri’s words also rang in his ears. Poor Grandfather Dobri! Pushed out into the street, struck hard on the head, his eyes tearing up from illness, or anger, or pity, the poor man kept speaking up in a broken voice: “But, Mr. Chief... wasn't it supposed to be... this here, weren't they supposed to be free... or something like that...” Poor Grandfather Dobri!...
After a few days, Gramatikov read the following telegram in one of the capital's newspapers:

“Sofia. To the Prime Minister. The elections were held in absolute silence and order. Elected: Ganyo Balkanski, Filyo Gochoolu, and Tanas Dochoolu, all of ours. The opposition candidates failed disgracefully. As soon as the voters appeared with music at their head, their gang scattered. The whole city is celebrating. Long live His Royal Highness. Ganyo Balkanski”

The letter to Gramatikov, which we mentioned above, ended with these words: “And what will the people say, what will they do? A curious question! You used to tell me once that you still believe in the Bulgarian people. Come on! Don’t mock me! In whom do you believe? In this slave tribe that endures all this? See it depicted in its representatives.”

The people, in whom you believe, is a slave, I tell you, a slave; enslavement is bliss for him, tyranny a blessing, servility heroism, the contemptuous snoring from above — music! And yet this people is wretched and unhappy, thrice unhappy! Beaten by fate, condemned to suffer and to toil for others, tortured by enemies, and even more so by friends and saviors, he had not a single firm point upon which to rest his gaze, a handle to lean upon, he has lost faith in himself and in his fate and has become so “practical” and sober, sober to the point of insensibility. Without help, without counsel, crushed and torn apart externally and internally, here he is, a mournful remnant of olden times, scattered by storms...
Is there anyone to revive it, to pull it along after them? — Ideals? — Vanity, wind!...
